Startup SaaS Frontend Development Enterprise Software Product Management Access Control Isn’t Just a Backend Problem Virendra Patil 4 min read · Oct 16, 2026 -- Listen Share Part 7 of “The Hidden Cost of Bad Frontend,” a series for founders and product leaders Press enter or click to view image in full size You’re closing your biggest deal yet: a 500-seat enterprise contract. Then their IT team sends over the security questionnaire: “Can we define custom roles?” “Can we restrict billing to finance users only?” “Can we give contractors read-only access?” “Can different departments see different features?” Your backend team says the data is protected. That’s great. But when you ask the frontend team how long it would take to show different screens, buttons and menus to different roles , the answer is: “We’d have to go through every page.” The deal slips by a quarter. The hidden cost Access control is usually treated as a backend concern, and the backend must enforce it. But the frontend decides what each user experiences , and when it’s built carelessly, the costs show up across the business: Enterprise deals stall. Roles and permissions are standard requirements in larger deals. “Coming soon” sends buyers toward competitors who already have it. Confusing user experience. Users see buttons they can’t use, click them, and get an error. They feel the product is broken, not that they lack permission. Pricing plans are hard to sell. If you can’t easily show or hide features per plan, you can’t easily create a “Pro” tier, run a trial or upsell. Every new role becomes a project. Adding a “Viewer” or “Auditor” role means editing dozens of files and hoping nothing is missed. Access control done well isn’t just a security checkbox. It’s what lets you sell the same product to a 5-person startup and a 5,000-person enterprise. What’s actually happening Think of an office building with keycards. The bad version: every door has its own guard holding a handwritten list of names. When someone gets promoted, you have to visit every guard and update every list. Some guards get missed. Some lists say different things. The good version: there’s one central system. Each keycard carries a set of permissions . Every door simply asks “does this card have access?” Change someone’s role in one place, and every door updates instantly. Most early apps are built the first way, with if (user.role === 'admin') checks scattered across hundreds of components. Mature apps use the second: one permission system that every screen asks. The “aha” moment: scattered checks vs. one permission system ❌ Role checks scattered everywhere // InvoicePage.tsx {user.role === 'admin' && <Button>Delete Invoice</Button>} // Sidebar.tsx {(user.role === 'admin' || user.role === 'manager') && <Link to="/billing">Billing</Link>} // ReportsPage.tsx {user.role !== 'viewer' && <ExportButton />} // …repeated in 80 more places, each slightly different Now a customer asks for a new “Finance” role that can see billing but not delete invoices. Someone has to find and update every one of those checks, without missing any. ✅ Ask about permissions, not roles // modules/auth/permissions.ts: one source of truth export const PERMISSIONS = { INVOICE_VIEW: 'invoice:view', INVOICE_DELETE: 'invoice:delete', REPORT_EXPORT: 'report:export', } as const; // modules/auth/hooks/usePermission.ts export function usePermission(permission: Permission) { const { user } = useAuth(); return user.permissions.includes(permission); // provided by the backend } // modules/auth/components/Can.tsx export function Can({ permission, children }: CanProps) { return usePermission(permission) ? <>{children}</> : null; } // Anywhere in the app: readable, consistent, typed <Can permission={PERMISSIONS.INVOICE_DELETE}> <Button danger>{t('billing.deleteInvoice')}</Button> </Can> // Whole routes protected the same way <Route path="/billing" element={<RequirePermission permission={PERMISSIONS.INVOICE_VIEW}><BillingPage /></RequirePermission>} /> Now the new “Finance” role is a backend configuration change : give it invoice:view but not invoice:delete . The frontend adapts automatically, with no code changes on any screen. The same pattern works for plans and feature access : <Can permission={FEATURES.ADVANCED_REPORTS}> <AdvancedReports /> </Can> // Not on the plan? Show an upgrade prompt instead of a hidden dead end. That turns access control into a revenue tool : trials, tiers and upsells become product configuration instead of engineering projects. ⚠️ Important: hiding a button in the frontend is about user experience , not security. The backend must still check every permission on every request. The frontend makes the product clear and pleasant; the backend keeps it safe. You need both. What good teams do differently Check permissions, not role names. Roles change and multiply. Permissions (“can delete invoice”) stay stable. Keep one source of truth. Permissions come from the backend and are read through one hook or component, never re-implemented on each screen. Protect routes, not just buttons.
